a: Of David, the LORD's servant
t: A title from 2 Samuel, and the verse numbers
p: The heading tells the same story as 2 Samuel 22:1. In Hebrew Bibles it is verse 1, so every verse number is one higher.
b: The heading is almost word for word the narrator's line in 2 Samuel 22:1, with two additions: "For the music director" and "the LORD's servant". Only here and in the title of Psalm 36 is David given that title in a psalm heading; it belongs to Moses (Deuteronomy 34:5) and Joshua (Joshua 24:29). A note on numbering for Psalms 18–30: this site, like most English Bibles, calls the title verse 0. The Hebrew Bible counts the title as verse 1, so Psalm 18:1 here is 18:2 in a Hebrew Bible, and Psalm 18 has 51 verses there. The Greek and Latin Bibles number this psalm 17; their number for each psalm is given on its chapter page.
orig: לְעֶבֶד יְהוָה לְדָוִד (le'eved YHWH ledavid), 'of the servant of the LORD, of David'

a: from the hand of Saul
p: The same poem closes David's story in 2 Samuel 22 and stands here in the Psalter, with small differences throughout.
b: Psalm 18 and 2 Samuel 22 are two copies of one song. The Plain here uses the site's wording of 2 Samuel 22 wherever the Hebrew of the two copies agrees, so the reader can see where they part. The differences are many but small: a missing opening line in Samuel, a word heard differently ("swooped" or "came into view", 18:10), an extra line in one copy or the other (18:13; 18:35). The chapter page sets them side by side. Most scholars think both copies go back to one written poem that was copied separately for a long time, one in the history of David and one in the temple's song book.

a: I love you, LORD, my strength.
p: The verb usually means 'have pity'. Only here does a person use it for loving God.
b: Hebrew has a common word for love, 'ahav. David does not use it. He says 'erchamkha, from racham, the root of the word for a mother's womb and for compassion (rachamim). In its usual form it means "have pity on", and God is nearly always the one who pities. This simple form occurs only here in the Bible, and it gives the line a warm, close feel, like the love of family. The line is missing from 2 Samuel 22:2, which starts at "The LORD is my high cliff." Some scholars think the Psalm added it for worship; others think Samuel lost it.

a: I take shelter in him
p: The verb chasah, 'take refuge', is one of the Psalter's key words. Hebrews may quote this line.
b: Chasah means to run to a shelter, as people run to a rock or into the shade (Judges 9:15; Isaiah 30:2). It is one of the most common verbs of faith in the Psalms (2:12; 5:11; 25:20). Here the shelter is God himself, named with a string of soldier's words: cliff, fortress, rock, shield, horn, high tower. Hebrews 2:13 puts the words "I will trust in him" into the mouth of Jesus. Those words match Isaiah 8:17 in the Greek, and also the Greek of 2 Samuel 22:3, the copy of this verse, so the writer may have both passages in mind.

a: Death's ropes closed around me
p: The same Hebrew letters can mean 'ropes' or 'labor pains'. The Greek took the second, and Acts follows it.
b: Chevlei mavet can be read as "ropes of death" or "pains of death", since chevel means a cord and chevel, with other vowels, means a labor pain. The next verse pairs "the ropes of Sheol" with "snares", so the Plain takes ropes, a hunter's noose. The Greek translators read "pangs of death" (ōdines thanatou). Peter's speech in Acts 2:24 speaks of God loosing the "pangs of death" from Jesus, words that come from this Greek line or from Psalm 116:3. The copy in 2 Samuel 22:5 has a third word, "breakers", the waves of death (see the variant).

a: The earth heaved and quaked
t: God comes down in the storm
p: Earthquake, smoke, fire, darkness and thunder are the signs of God's coming, as at Sinai.
b: From here to 18:15 the poem describes God's coming in the language of a great storm and earthquake. These are the signs of Sinai (Exodus 19:16–18) and of the old battle songs (Judges 5:4–5; Habakkuk 3:3–15). Canaanite poems describe the storm god Baal in a similar way (see the note at 2 Samuel 22:9). The question for readers is what David saw. Some take the storm as the poet's way of saying that God himself fought for him in a real battle; others think a real storm broke over a battle, as at Gibeon (Joshua 10:11) or at Mizpah (1 Samuel 7:10). Either way the point is that the LORD of the universe answered one man's cry from his temple.
r: Exodus 19:16–18; Judges 5:4–5; Habakkuk 3:3–15; Joshua 10:11; 1 Samuel 7:10; 2 Samuel 22:9

a: Riding a cherub
p: God rides the winged cherub as a storm chariot, the same creature carved over the ark.
b: A cherub (plural cherubim) was a winged guardian creature, part animal and part human, carved over the ark and in the temple (Exodus 25:18–22; 1 Kings 6:23–28). The LORD was "enthroned on the cherubim" (1 Samuel 4:4). Here the throne takes flight. Ezekiel sees the same creatures carrying God's chariot throne (Ezekiel 1; Ezekiel 10). The cherubs of the Bible are nothing like the chubby babies of later art.
r: Exodus 25:18–22; 1 Kings 6:23–28; 1 Samuel 4:4; Ezekiel 1:4–28; Ezekiel 10:1–22; Psalm 104:3

a: He made darkness his hiding place
p: God both comes near and stays hidden. The Psalm adds 'hiding place', a word Psalm 91 and Psalm 27 use for shelter.
b: The Samuel copy says only that God "wrapped himself in darkness" (2 Samuel 22:12). The Psalm adds sitro, "his hiding place". At Sinai Moses went into the thick darkness where God was (Exodus 20:21), and Solomon said the LORD chose to live in thick darkness (1 Kings 8:12). The same word that hides God here shelters the believer elsewhere: "the hidden part of his tent" (27:5) and the shelter of the Most High (Psalm 91:1). The God who hides himself in the storm hides his servant from it.

a: he shot lightning in plenty
p: The short word rav can mean 'many' or 'he shot'. The Samuel copy has a single lightning.
b: The Hebrew reads uveraqim rav, "and lightnings, rav". Rav usually means "many" or "much", which gives "lightnings in plenty". But a rare verb ravav means "to shoot" (Genesis 49:23), and the line is about arrows, so many scholars read "he shot lightning". The Plain keeps both: "he shot lightning in plenty". The Samuel copy has just "lightning" (2 Samuel 22:15). The "arrows" in the first line are the lightning bolts, a common picture (Psalm 77:17; Psalm 144:6; Habakkuk 3:11).
orig: וּבְרָקִים רָב (uveraqim rav), 'and lightnings, many / he shot'

a: at your rebuke, LORD
t: The rebuke that drives back the sea
p: God 'rebukes' the waters and they run. The Psalm turns to speak to God here; the Samuel copy does not.
b: Ge'arah, "rebuke", is the shout of a master at an unruly animal. In the Bible God rebukes the sea (Psalm 104:7; Psalm 106:9; Nahum 1:4), as at the Sea of Reeds, and its floor is laid bare. The Samuel copy keeps talking about God ("when the LORD rebuked"); the Psalm suddenly turns and speaks to him ("your rebuke, LORD ... your nose"). Readers of the Gospels hear this behind the scene where Jesus "rebuked" the wind and the sea and they went calm (Mark 4:39).
orig: מִגַּעֲרָתְךָ יְהוָה (migga'aratkha YHWH), 'from your rebuke, LORD'
r: Psalm 104:7; Psalm 106:9; Nahum 1:4; Exodus 15:8; Mark 4:39; 2 Samuel 22:16

a: he pulled me from great waters
p: 'Great waters' in the Psalms are more than a flood: they stand for the powers of chaos and death.
b: Mayim rabbim, "great" or "many waters", is a fixed phrase in Hebrew poetry for the deep, wild waters that God alone rules (29:3; Psalm 93:4; Psalm 144:7). In the old Near Eastern stories the sea is a monster the storm god must defeat. In Israel's poems the sea is a creature, but it still stands for death and disorder. So the rescue is more than from drowning: God reaches down from the heights into the chaos and pulls one man out of it.

a: he paid me back for my clean hands
t: How can a king claim clean hands?
p: David's claim to be righteous sounds strange after Bathsheba. Readers explain it in several ways.
b: This puzzle is also raised at 2 Samuel 22:21. In the Psalter the claim is read in several ways. Covenant loyalty: "righteousness" means the king did not turn to other gods or break faith with the LORD (18:21–22), not that he never sinned. Before the enemy: in his quarrel with Saul, David was the innocent one (1 Samuel 24:11; 1 Samuel 26:23). A royal liturgy: sung in the temple, the words state what every king of David's line was meant to be (Deuteronomy 17:18–20). Christian readers such as Augustine heard the voice of Christ, the one king whose hands were wholly clean, speaking with his people.

a: I have not put his rules away from me
p: The pair mishpatim and chuqqot is the language of Deuteronomy. The Psalm's verb differs slightly from Samuel's.
b: "Rulings" (mishpatim) and "rules" (chuqqot) are the site's standard words for the pair Deuteronomy uses for the whole law (Deuteronomy 4:1; Deuteronomy 5:1). The Psalm says "I have not put away from me" (lo' 'asir menni); the Samuel copy says "I have not swerved from it" (lo' 'asur mimmennah, 2 Samuel 22:23). The two verbs look alike in Hebrew. The king is the model Israelite who keeps the law of Moses always "before" him, as the law of the king commands (Deuteronomy 17:19).

a: You light my lamp, LORD
p: A lamp kept burning stood for a family line that does not die out. God promised David a lamp.
b: A lamp in the house meant someone still lived there; a lamp put out meant the family was gone (Job 18:5–6; Proverbs 13:9). God promised to give David "a lamp" in Jerusalem, a son on his throne, even when his heirs failed (1 Kings 11:36; 1 Kings 15:4; 2 Kings 8:19), and Psalm 132:17 speaks of a lamp God sets up for his anointed king. When David's men would not let him go to battle any more, they said it was so he would not put out "the lamp of Israel" (2 Samuel 21:17). The Samuel copy says God is the lamp (2 Samuel 22:29); the Psalm says God lights it.
orig: תָּאִיר נֵרִי (ta'ir neri), 'you light my lamp'
r: 1 Kings 11:36; 1 Kings 15:4; 2 Kings 8:19; Psalm 132:17; 2 Samuel 21:17; 2 Samuel 22:29; Job 18:5–6

a: and your gentleness makes me great
p: The word 'anvah usually means a person's humility. Here it is God's: he bends down to lift the king.
b: 'Anvatkha is "your humility", "your gentleness" or "your stooping down". The same word describes Moses, the humblest man on earth (Numbers 12:3), and the humble whom God saves (18:27). Applied to God it is bold: the king's greatness comes from God's willingness to bend low. Psalm 113:6 says the same thing in other words. The Greek has "your discipline set me up straight" and adds "your discipline will teach me", taking the word from a root meaning "to train" and translating it twice. The Samuel copy (2 Samuel 22:36) has "when you answer me" and lacks the line "your right hand holds me up".

a: from the feuds of the people
p: The king is saved from quarrels among his own people and made head over foreign nations.
b: "The people" ('am) in this line is probably Israel itself, as the Samuel copy makes clear with "my people" (2 Samuel 22:44). David's reign was torn by civil war: first with the house of Saul, then with Absalom and Sheba (2 Samuel 3:1; 2 Samuel 15–20). At the same time he made Moab, Aram, Ammon and Edom pay him tribute (2 Samuel 8). Later readers, after the kings were gone, heard a promise that a son of David would one day rule the nations (2:8; 72:8–11).

a: I will give you thanks among the nations
p: Paul quotes this line in Romans 15:9 as the first of four texts showing that Gentiles were meant to praise God.
b: In Romans 15:8–12 Paul strings together four Old Testament texts in which the nations praise the God of Israel: this verse, Deuteronomy 32:43, Psalm 117:1 and Isaiah 11:10. He reads the king's thanks "among the nations" as the voice of Christ, the son of David, praising God in the middle of a people now made up of Jews and Gentiles. For the song's first hearers it was a king's vow to praise the LORD in front of the nations he had defeated. Both readings are given at 2 Samuel 22:50.

a: to David and his line for all time
t: The anointed one and his line
p: The song ends with God's promise to David's line. Jews and Christians both hear the Messiah in it.
b: The last line repeats God's promise to David in 2 Samuel 7:12–16: loyal love (hesed) to David "and his line for all time." The king is called God's "anointed" (meshicho), the word that later gave us "messiah". When the kings had ended, Jewish readers held on to the verse as a promise of the coming son of David, and it is said near the end of the grace after meals. Christians read it as fulfilled in Jesus, "the son of David" (Matthew 1:1). In this copy the written and read Hebrew both mean "he makes great"; the Samuel copy has "tower" in its spoken text (see 2 Samuel 22:51).

a: The heavens keep recounting God's glory
p: The sky preaches without words. Paul uses this idea, and the church built a whole teaching on it.
b: The first half of the psalm (19:1–6) says that the sky itself tells of God, day and night, to every land. Paul makes the same point in Romans 1:19–20: what can be known of God's power is seen in the things he made. Christian teachers called this "general revelation" or "the book of nature", beside the "book of Scripture" of 19:7–11. They disagree on how far it goes. Thomas Aquinas held that reason can know God exists from creation; Calvin said the world is a theater of God's glory but that sinners need Scripture as "spectacles" to read it (Institutes 1.5–6). The psalm itself puts the two side by side and does not rank them.

a: the sky's dome
p: Raqia', the 'firmament', is the beaten-out dome of Genesis 1. The psalm uses the old picture of the sky.
b: Raqia' comes from a verb for hammering out metal (Exodus 39:3). In Genesis 1:6–8 God makes the raqia' to hold back the waters above, and this site translates it "dome" there. The older English "firmament" comes from the Latin firmamentum, "a strong support". The psalm speaks in the picture of the world that its first hearers shared. Its point is not the shape of the sky but whose work it is: the God it calls El, the plain word for God, here, before it turns to the personal name, the LORD, in 19:7.

a: No speech, no words
p: Is the sky's voice not heard at all, or heard in every language? The Hebrew allows both.
b: The Hebrew is three short clauses: "there is no speech, and there are no words; their voice is not heard." Most modern translators read a paradox: the heavens speak without sound. The KJV read it the other way: "There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard," that is, they are heard in every tongue. Joseph Addison's hymn "The Spacious Firmament on High" (1712) put the first reading into verse: what though no real voice nor sound is heard, in reason's ear they all rejoice. Both readings lead to 19:4: the message goes out everywhere.
orig: אֵין־אֹמֶר וְאֵין דְּבָרִים בְּלִי נִשְׁמָע קוֹלָם

a: There he has set up a tent for the sun,
t: The sun as runner and bridegroom
p: Israel's neighbors worshiped the sun as a god of justice. Here the sun is a creature with a tent God pitched.
b: In Babylon the sun god Shamash was the judge who sees everything, and hymns praise his daily course over the earth. In Egypt the sun god Ra crossed the sky by day. Psalm 19 uses the same pictures, a bridegroom and a strong runner, but the sun has no name and no power of its own. God pitched its tent. Many critical scholars think 19:1–6 was an older hymn about the sun, joined to a poem on the law (19:7–14); some suggest the link was deliberate, since the sun god was the god of justice and the psalm gives that role to the LORD's law, from which "nothing hides" (19:6). The likeness of language is real; whether the psalm answers sun worship on purpose is a guess.

a: like a bridegroom from the wedding room
p: The word for 'wedding room' is chuppah, the name of the canopy under which Jewish couples still marry.
b: Chuppah is the bridal room or canopy (Joel 2:16). Jewish weddings today still take place under a chuppah. The sun comes out at dawn like a groom after his wedding night, glowing and glad. The Greek and Latin of the second line call the sun a "giant" (Latin gigas), and from the fourth century Christians sang the verse at Christmas: Ambrose's hymn Veni, Redemptor gentium pictures Christ coming out of the bridal room of Mary's womb as a "giant of two natures". Later the verse was also read of Christ rising at dawn on Easter.

a: The LORD's law is flawless
p: In three verses the psalm names God's word six ways and uses the name the LORD six times.
b: Verses 19:7–9 are built from six short pairs. Each names God's word: torah "law" (also "teaching, instruction"), 'edut "decree", piqqudim "orders", mitsvah "command", "the fear of the LORD", and mishpatim "rulings". Each is "of the LORD", and each gets a quality and an effect: it revives, makes wise, gladdens, gives light, lasts, is right. Psalm 119 builds its whole 176 verses from the same list. Up to here the psalm called God only El; now the personal name, the LORD, comes six times in a row (seven with 19:14), as if the God of the sky had come near in his law.

a: it brings the soul back to life
p: The phrase means to bring back life and strength, as food does for a starving person.
b: Meshivat nafesh, literally "causing the soul to return", is used of food that brings a fainting person back to life (Lamentations 1:11; Lamentations 1:19), and of a grandson who renews a grandmother's life (Ruth 4:15). Nefesh is not a ghostly part of a person but the living self, breath and appetite and life. The LORD's law does for the whole person what bread does for the starving. A related phrase comes in 23:3, where the shepherd "brings my life back".

a: than what drips from the comb
p: God's words taste like honey in Ezekiel and Psalm 119 too; Jewish children once got honey on their first school day.
b: Honey from the comb was the sweetest thing an Israelite knew. Psalm 119:103 and Ezekiel 3:3 use the same picture: God's words are sweet in the mouth. A medieval Jewish custom made the image literal: when a small boy began to study the Torah, the letters were written on a slate and covered with honey for him to lick, so that the law would be sweet to him. Revelation 10:9–10 turns the picture: a scroll sweet in the mouth and bitter in the stomach.

a: Clear me of faults I cannot see.
p: The law of Moses had offerings for sins done in ignorance. The psalmist asks God to cover even those.
b: Shegi'ot, "slips, errors", comes from the verb used in Leviticus and Numbers for sins done without knowing (shegagah; Leviticus 4:2; Numbers 15:27–29). "Faults I cannot see" (nistarot, "hidden things") are sins hidden from the sinner himself. The next verse turns to the opposite kind: arrogant or willful sins (19:13), done "with a high hand", for which the law gave no offering (Numbers 15:30–31). The psalmist asks God to deal with both kinds, the sins he cannot see and the pride that would make him sin on purpose.

a: May what my mouth says
p: Jews say this verse at the end of the daily Amidah, and many Christian preachers say it before a sermon.
b: Leratson, "for acceptance", is the word used for an offering God accepts (Leviticus 1:3; Leviticus 22:20). The psalmist offers his words and thoughts as a sacrifice. The Talmud (Berakhot 9b) says this verse is said at the end of the Amidah, the standing prayer said three times a day, and it is still said there today. Many Christian ministers pray it before they preach, and it has been set to music often.

a: In your day of trouble, may the LORD answer you
p: The people pray for their king as he offers sacrifice before going to war.
b: The "you" of 20:1–5 is the king, and the speakers are the people, perhaps with a priest leading. The king has brought grain and burnt offerings (20:3), as Saul did before battle (1 Samuel 13:9–12) and as Jehoshaphat's army prayed and sang before facing Moab and Ammon (2 Chronicles 20:5–21). Then a single voice says, "Now I know it" (20:6): many scholars think a priest or prophet has just given an answer from God, like Jahaziel's message in 2 Chronicles 20:14–17. Jews say this psalm in the weekday morning service, near the end, as a prayer in time of trouble.

a: the name of Jacob's God
p: In the Psalms God's 'name' stands for God himself present to help.
b: The psalm calls on "the name" three times (20:1; 20:5; 20:7). In Deuteronomy God puts his name in the place he chooses (Deuteronomy 12:5), and Solomon prays toward the temple as the place where God said, "My name will be there" (1 Kings 8:29). To trust the name is to trust God as he has made himself known and present, not a magic word. "Jacob's God" recalls the patriarch who was answered "on the day of my trouble" (Genesis 35:3), almost the words of this verse.

a: find your burnt offering rich
p: The verb means 'to make fat'. God is asked to treat the king's offering as rich and fully acceptable.
b: Yedashneh comes from deshen, "fat" and also the fatty ashes left on the altar (Leviticus 6:10). To "make fat" an offering is to count it rich and accept it. "Grain offerings" (minchot) and "burnt offering" ('olah) are the regular names of two kinds of sacrifice (Leviticus 1–2).

a: the LORD has rescued his anointed
t: Who speaks, and why the past tense?
p: A new voice and a sudden 'has rescued' suggest an answer from God has come between 20:5 and 20:6.
b: Up to 20:5 a group prays ("Let us cheer"); now one voice says "I know" and speaks of the rescue as done. Form critics such as Gunkel and Mowinckel took this as a sign that a priest or temple prophet gave an oracle after the sacrifice, and the speaker answers with certainty. Others think the king himself speaks, or that the past tense is the "perfect of confidence", speaking of a future act as already done because God has promised it. "His anointed" is the king (see 18:50).

a: These have chariots, and those have horses
t: Trust is not in the Hebrew
p: Many English Bibles say 'Some trust in chariots'. The Hebrew has no verb in the first line at all.
b: The Hebrew says only "These in chariots, and these in horses, but we in the name of the LORD our God nazkir." The verb nazkir means "we call to mind", "we invoke" or "we boast of" (Exodus 23:13; Isaiah 26:13). The word "trust" that many translations supply is a fair guess at the sense, but it is not written. The verse echoes the law of the king, who must not pile up horses (Deuteronomy 17:16), and Isaiah's warning against those who rely on Egypt's chariots (Isaiah 31:1).
orig: וַאֲנַחְנוּ בְּשֵׁם־יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ נַזְכִּיר (va'anachnu beshem-YHWH 'eloheinu nazkir)

a: the king is glad because of your strength
p: The Targum turns 'the king' in this psalm into 'King Messiah'. Rashi notes that reading and prefers David.
b: Psalm 21 thanks God for answering the prayer of Psalm 20: the king has been given what his heart wanted (21:2; compare 20:4). The Targum, the Aramaic translation read in the synagogue, renders "the king" in 21:1 and 21:7 as "King Messiah". Rashi, in the eleventh century, mentions that the rabbis read the psalm of the Messiah, and himself explains it of David. Christian readers have heard in it the risen Christ crowned and given "life ... forever" (21:4), and the Book of Common Prayer appoints it for Ascension Day.

a: a crown of refined gold
p: David put on the gold crown of the king of Rabbah after his victory over Ammon.
b: 'Ateret paz is a crown of refined, pure gold. When David captured Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, he took the gold crown from its king's head, weighing a talent, and it was set on his own (2 Samuel 12:30). A crown was also part of Joash's coronation (2 Kings 11:12). Some scholars think this psalm was sung at a coronation or on the anniversary of one; others tie it to a victory, as 21:8–12 suggest.

a: long days, on and on forever
p: Court language wished the king long life. Later readers heard more: life that does not end.
b: "May the king live forever!" was what people said to kings (1 Kings 1:31; Daniel 2:4; Nehemiah 2:3). Here the request is granted: "long days" ('orekh yamim), "forever and ever". The first sense is a long reign and a lasting dynasty (2 Samuel 7:16). The Talmud (Sukkah 52a) puts this verse in the mouth of the Messiah, son of David, who asks God for life and is given it. Christians read it of Christ, raised to a life that death no longer rules (Romans 6:9).
orig: אֹרֶךְ יָמִים עוֹלָם וָעֶד ('orekh yamim 'olam va'ed)

a: For you make him a blessing forever
p: The words recall God's promise to Abraham: 'you will be a blessing'.
b: The Hebrew says "you set him as blessings forever". It can mean "you make him most blessed", but it also echoes God's words to Abraham, "be a blessing" (Genesis 12:2), and the hope that the nations will bless themselves by Israel's king (Psalm 72:17). The second line says why: he is glad "before your face", in God's presence.

a: Your hand will track down all your enemies
p: From 21:8 the speaker addresses either the king or God. The answer changes how fierce the lines sound.
b: In 21:1–7 the people speak to God about the king. In 21:8–12 "you" may be the king (so many modern scholars, since 21:9 then names the LORD in the third person) or God (so the Targum and many older readers). If it is the king, these are a court's wishes for victory over his foes. If it is God, they look forward to God's judgment on those who "stretched out evil against you" (21:11). Either way the speakers hand the fight to God's power, not their own (21:13). For how Jews and Christians pray such fierce lines, see the page on the curse psalms.

a: like a fiery furnace
p: A tannur was a clay oven. The enemies will burn like the inside of one.
b: Tannur is the round clay oven used for baking bread, heated red-hot from inside (Leviticus 2:4; Hosea 7:4–7). Malachi 4:1 uses the same picture for the day of the LORD, "burning like an oven". The phrase "at the time you show your face" means when the king (or God) appears for battle, with the face as a sign of presence.

a: You will make them show you their shoulders
p: Shekhem, 'shoulder', is an idiom for the enemy's back as they run away.
b: To "set them shoulder" is to make them turn their backs and flee (compare 18:40, "You gave me my enemies' necks"). The Greek has "you will make them a back". The second line pictures an archer aiming at the faces of those who still stand. In Exodus 23:27 God promises to make Israel's enemies turn their backs, using a related phrase.

a: On "The Doe of the Dawn."
p: Probably the name of a tune. The Greek heard 'help at dawn'; the rabbis saw Queen Esther.
b: 'Al 'ayyelet hashachar is most likely the first words of a song whose tune this psalm used, like "Lilies" (45:0) or "A Silent Dove Far Away" (56:0). The Greek translators read 'eyalut, "help, strength" (the word in 22:19, "my strength"), and wrote "for the help at dawn". The Talmud (Megillah 15b) says Esther prayed 22:1 as she went in to the king uninvited; Yoma 29a and the Midrash on Psalms compare her to the dawn. Christian writers took the doe and the dawn as Christ, rising early on the first day.

a: My God, my God
p: Jesus cries the first line of this psalm from the cross in Aramaic, in Mark and Matthew.
b: In Mark 15:34 Jesus, at about three in the afternoon, cries out "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?", the first line of this psalm in Aramaic, and Mark translates it. Matthew 27:46 gives the start in Hebrew form, "Eli, Eli". Some bystanders thought he was calling Elijah (Eli sounds like Eliyyahu). These are the only words from the cross in Mark and Matthew. The Aramaic verb shevaq, "leave", is the one the Targum uses for this verse. Luke and John do not report the cry; they record other words.

a: why have you abandoned me?
p: Did Jesus feel cut off from God, or was he praying a psalm that ends in praise? Christians answer in different ways.
b: 'Azav is the ordinary verb for leaving someone behind or abandoning them (Genesis 2:24; Psalm 27:10). In the psalm the speaker is a faithful person who still says "my God" while he feels deserted. Readers of the Gospels take Jesus' use of it in three main ways. He quoted the opening of the whole psalm, as Jews named a passage by its first words, so the cry includes its ending of praise and vindication (22:22–31). He truly felt abandoned, bearing sin and its separation from God (Galatians 3:13; 2 Corinthians 5:21). He spoke in our place, taking on the human cry of every sufferer without ever ceasing to be one with the Father. The three can be combined, and churches weigh them differently: see "Where Christians differ" on the chapter page.

a: from the words I roar out
p: Sha'agah is a lion's roar. The sufferer roars at God, and soon lions roar at him.
b: Sha'agah is used for the roar of a lion (Job 4:10; Isaiah 5:29) and for a human groan of pain (Job 3:24; Psalm 32:3). The speaker's prayer is not polite. Later in the psalm his enemies are "a lion ripping prey and roaring" (22:13), with the same root. The Greek read a different word, shegagah, "sin done in error", and translated "the words of my transgressions" (see the variant).

a: sit on Israel's praises as your throne
p: The LORD is usually enthroned on the cherubim. Here his throne is Israel's songs. The Hebrew can be divided other ways.
b: The Hebrew is four words: "and you holy, sitting, praises of Israel." The usual reading is that God sits enthroned on Israel's praises, as he "sits on the cherubim" above the ark (1 Samuel 4:4; Psalm 99:1). The accents of the Hebrew can also give "you are the Holy One, enthroned, the praise of Israel" (compare Deuteronomy 10:21, "he is your praise"). The Greek has "you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel." The KJV's "thou that inhabitest the praises of Israel" became a favorite text in modern worship movements for the idea that praise brings God's presence. The psalm's point is narrower: the God of Israel's songs and history seems absent from the singer.

a: But I am a worm and not a man
p: A worm is the lowest of creatures. A popular sermon about a crimson 'dye worm' reads more into the word than is there.
b: The sufferer feels less than human, the way Isaiah calls exiled Israel "worm Jacob" (Isaiah 41:14) and Job's friend calls man a maggot (Job 25:6). The word tola'at also names the scale insect from which crimson dye was made (Exodus 25:4, "crimson" is tola'at shani). A widely shared modern devotional says the psalm means that insect, which dies on a tree and stains it red, as a picture of the cross. The psalm does not say so, and the insect's life does not match the story told about it; the word here simply means a worm, something crushed underfoot. The second half of the verse fits the servant of Isaiah 53:3, despised and rejected.

a: shake their heads
p: Matthew and Mark describe passers-by at the cross shaking their heads, as here.
b: Shaking the head and making faces was the ancient gesture of scorn at someone ruined (Lamentations 2:15; Job 16:4; Psalm 109:25). Mark 15:29 and Matthew 27:39 say that passers-by at the cross insulted Jesus, "shaking their heads". Matthew 27:43 then gives the chief priests' taunt in words close to 22:8. The Gospel writers do not stop to say "this fulfilled"; they tell the scene in the psalm's own language and expect readers to hear it.

a: Roll it onto the LORD!
p: The Hebrew gol means 'roll'. The mockers throw the sufferer's faith back at him.
b: Gol 'el-YHWH is literally "roll to the LORD". The Masoretic pointing gol makes it a command, "Roll it onto the LORD!", the mockers' sarcastic advice, and the Plain follows it; "it" is supplied. Read with other vowels (gal) it is a description, "he rolled it onto the LORD", which is how the Greek and Syriac took it (see the variant). The same verb comes in "roll your way onto the LORD" (Psalm 37:5; Proverbs 16:3). The Greek has "he hoped in the Lord", and Matthew 27:43 puts a similar line in the mouths of the leaders at the cross: he trusted in God; let God save him now, if he wants him. The Wisdom of Solomon 2:18, a book in the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testament, has the wicked plot in the same way against "the righteous man": if he is God's son, God will help him.
r: Psalm 37:5; Proverbs 16:3; Matthew 27:43; Wisdom of Solomon 2:16–20

a: you taught me trust at my mother's breasts
p: The verb means 'make me trust' or 'keep me safe'. The line is cited in Christian debates over infant faith.
b: Mavtichi is the causative form of batach, "to trust": "the one who makes me trust". Many scholars take it more simply as "you kept me safe" at my mother's breast, since batach also means to be secure. Either way the sufferer appeals to God as the midwife at his birth and the one he has belonged to since infancy (22:10; compare Psalm 71:6; Jeremiah 1:5). Because the verse speaks of a baby's trust, it is cited in arguments over whether infants can have faith; see "Where Christians differ" on the chapter page.

a: the mighty ones of Bashan
p: Bashan, east of the Sea of Galilee, was famous for its rich pastures and huge cattle.
b: Bashan is the high plateau east of the Sea of Galilee, today's Golan and the land beyond it, with good volcanic soil and grass. Its cattle were proverbial for size and strength (Deuteronomy 32:14; Ezekiel 39:18), and Amos calls the pampered women of Samaria "cows of Bashan" (Amos 4:1). The enemies in 22:12–21 come as a zoo of beasts: bulls, a lion, dogs, wild oxen. The pictures show how the sufferer feels, powerless before brute strength.

a: I am poured out like water
p: Christian readers have found the cross in these lines. The Hebrew uses common pictures of terror and weakness.
b: Verses 22:14–17 describe a body coming apart: poured out like water, bones out of joint, heart melting, mouth dry, bones that can be counted. Hebrew poetry uses these pictures for fear and collapse: hearts melt (Joshua 7:5), life is water spilled on the ground (2 Samuel 14:14), bones shake (Psalm 6:2). Many Christians, from the church fathers to modern devotional writers, have read them as an exact picture of crucifixion, with its strained joints, thirst and exposure. Jewish readers and many scholars answer that the lines describe a sick or persecuted person in standard poetic terms. Both sides agree the psalm describes someone near death and stripped of all dignity.

a: My strength has dried out
p: The Hebrew says 'my strength'; many scholars think it was 'my palate', which fits the tongue in the next line.
b: "My strength (kochi) has dried out like broken pottery" is an odd image. Changing the order of two letters gives chikki, "my palate", the roof of the mouth, which pairs well with "my tongue is glued to my gums". Many modern translations follow that change; the Plain keeps the Hebrew. John 19:28 says Jesus, knowing all was done, said "I am thirsty" so that the Scripture would be fulfilled. John does not say which Scripture; this verse and Psalm 69:21 are the usual suggestions.

a: death's dust
p: Dust is where humans came from and where the dead go.
b: God made the first human from the dust of the ground and said he would return to it (Genesis 2:7; Genesis 3:19). In the Psalms the dead are "those who go down to the dust" (22:29; 30:9). The startling part of the line is "you": the sufferer sees God's own hand in laying him down to die, and still prays to him.

a: For dogs are all around me
p: In Israel dogs were half-wild scavengers, not pets. Later readers took them as enemies or as foreign nations.
b: Dogs in the Bible are mostly street scavengers that eat what is left of the dead (1 Kings 14:11; 1 Kings 21:23). To be surrounded by dogs is to be treated as carrion before one is dead. Later Jewish readers such as Rashi took the beasts of this psalm as the nations that oppress Israel in exile; Christian readers took the dogs as the Gentile soldiers and the bulls as the leaders at the cross. In the psalm they are simply enemies too many to fight.

a: Like a lion
t: Lion or piercing: how each side argues
p: Jews and Christians have argued over the Hebrew 'like a lion' and the Greek 'they dug' since the second century.
b: Christian readers since Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 97–98, about AD 155) have read "they dug my hands and my feet", following the Greek, and seen the nails of the cross. They point to the oldest Hebrew copy, from Nahal Hever, which seems to have a verb here, and to the fact that "like a lion my hands and feet" has no verb. Jewish readers, with the Masoretic Text and the Targum, read "like a lion", the lion of 22:13 and 22:21, mauling the sufferer's limbs. Writers such as Isaac of Troki (Chizzuk Emunah, about 1594) answered that the Christian reading changes a letter, and that the psalm never mentions crucifixion. Many scholars think neither "like a lion" nor "pierced" is certain. The full evidence is in the variant.

a: over my clothing they throw lots
p: All four Gospels tell how soldiers divided Jesus' clothes. John quotes this verse and sees two acts in its two lines.
b: Clothes of an executed man went to the executioners. Mark 15:24, Matthew 27:35 and Luke 23:34 say the soldiers divided Jesus' clothes by lot, in the language of this verse. John 19:23–24 quotes it and treats the two lines as two events: the clothes were split four ways, and for the seamless tunic they threw lots. In Hebrew poetry the second line usually repeats the first in other words, so most readers of the psalm alone take it as one act. John's reading shows how closely the first Christians read the psalm alongside the story of the cross.

a: my one and only life
p: Yechidah, 'only one', is the word for Isaac, Abraham's only son. The Greek has monogenes.
b: Yechidati is literally "my only one", meaning "my life", the one life I have (also 35:17). The masculine yachid is used of Isaac, Abraham's "only" son (Genesis 22:2), and of an only child mourned (Jeremiah 6:26). The Greek translates monogenē, the word John uses for Jesus as God's "only" or "one-of-a-kind" Son (John 1:18; John 3:16). The church fathers noticed the link; in the psalm the word is the sufferer's own precious life.

a: the wild oxen
p: The KJV's 'unicorns' comes from the Greek. The re'em was the aurochs, a huge wild ox.
b: Re'em is the aurochs, the great wild ox of the ancient Near East, now extinct, hunted by Assyrian kings and pictured with two horns. The Greek translators, not knowing the animal, wrote monokerōs, "one-horned", and the Latin unicornis gave the KJV its "unicorns" (Numbers 23:22; Job 39:9–10). A side view of an aurochs on a carving, with one horn hiding the other, may lie behind the name.

a: you have answered me
p: In the Hebrew the prayer suddenly becomes 'you have answered me'. From here the psalm is praise.
b: The Hebrew does not finish the plea "save me ... from the horns of the wild oxen" with another request. It ends with one word, 'anitani, "you have answered me". The prayer breaks into thanks, and the next ten verses are praise (22:22–31). Some think a priest's word of assurance came between, as perhaps in 20:6. Others read the Greek "my lowliness", which keeps the plea going (see the variant). Read with the Hebrew, the psalm turns on this word, and Christian readers have heard in it the move from the cross to the resurrection.

a: I will spread the news of your name to my brothers
p: Hebrews 2:12 puts this verse in the mouth of Jesus, calling believers his brothers.
b: Hebrews 2:11–12 says Jesus is not ashamed to call those he makes holy his "brothers", and quotes this verse as his words: he will announce God's name to them and sing praise in the assembly. The Greek ekklēsia there, "assembly", is the word that came to mean "church". On Easter morning, too, Jesus calls the disciples "my brothers" (Matthew 28:10; John 20:17). In the psalm the rescued person keeps his vow by telling his story to the gathered worshipers.

a: I will pay what I vowed
p: A person rescued in answer to a vow brought a sacrifice and shared the meat with others.
b: Israelites in danger often vowed an offering if God saved them (1 Samuel 1:11; Jonah 2:9). When the answer came they "paid" the vow at the temple with a peace offering, much of whose meat was eaten the same day by the worshiper and his guests (Leviticus 7:11–18; Leviticus 22:21). That is why the next verse says "the humble will eat until they have enough": the poor are invited to the feast. Christian writers from Augustine on have seen in this meal a picture of the Lord's Supper, where the poor eat and are filled.

a: The far corners of the earth will remember
p: One man's rescue ends with every nation, the dead and the unborn praising God.
b: The praise grows in circles: the speaker's brothers (22:22), all Israel (22:23), the great assembly (22:25), the ends of the earth and every clan of the nations (22:27), the dead (22:29), and people not yet born (22:31). The hope that the nations will "turn" to the LORD is that of Isaiah 45:22 and Isaiah 49:6 and of God's promise that all the families of the earth will be blessed (Genesis 12:3). Christian readers saw this fulfilled as the gospel went to the Gentiles.

a: All the rich of the earth
p: The Hebrew 'the fat of the earth' is hard. Many read 'all who sleep in the earth', so that even the dead worship.
b: The Hebrew says "they have eaten and bowed down, all the fat ones of the earth", meaning the prosperous, who join the humble at the feast. The next line has "all who go down to the dust", the dying or the dead. Many scholars divide the letters differently: 'akh lo yishtachavu kol-yeshenei 'erets, "surely to him all who sleep in the earth will bow", which gives a better parallel and has the dead praising God, something the Psalms usually deny (6:5; 30:9; 88:10). If so, this is one of the boldest lines in the Old Testament, close to Daniel 12:2. The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: He did it!
p: Some preachers link this last line with Jesus' last word in John 19:30. The words differ, but the idea is close.
b: The psalm ends with one Hebrew word after "that": 'asah, "he has acted" or "he did it". The coming generation will be told what God has done. Some sermons say that Jesus' last cry in John 19:30, tetelestai, "it is finished", is this verse. The Greek of the psalm does not use that word, and John does not cite the psalm there. The thought is close, though: God has finished the rescue, and the news is for those not yet born. Read either way, the psalm that began "why have you abandoned me?" ends with "he did it".

a: The LORD is my shepherd
t: God the shepherd, the king the shepherd
p: Kings in the ancient Near East called themselves shepherds. Israel called God its shepherd, and Jesus took the title.
b: Hammurabi of Babylon calls himself the shepherd of his people in the prologue to his laws, and Egyptian and Assyrian kings used the same title. In Israel David was taken from the sheep to shepherd God's people (2 Samuel 5:2; Psalm 78:70–72). But the true shepherd is God: Jacob blesses "God, my shepherd from my first day until this day" (Genesis 48:15), and Ezekiel 34 condemns Israel's bad shepherds and promises that God himself will tend his flock. Jesus says, "I am the good shepherd" (John 10:11), and the New Testament calls him the great and chief shepherd (Hebrews 13:20; 1 Peter 5:4; Revelation 7:17). Psalm 23 is unusual in using the image of one person, "my" shepherd.
orig: יְהוָה רֹעִי (YHWH ro'i), 'the LORD, my shepherd'
r: Genesis 48:15; 2 Samuel 5:2; Psalm 80:1; Ezekiel 34:11–16; John 10:11–16; Hebrews 13:20; Revelation 7:17

a: I will never be in need
p: The verb 'lack' recalls Moses' words about Israel's forty years in the desert.
b: Lo' 'echsar, "I do not lack", uses the verb of Deuteronomy 2:7, where Moses reminds Israel of the forty years in the wilderness: "You have not lacked a thing" (Deuteronomy 2:7). Many readers hear the whole exodus behind the psalm: God leading his flock through the desert, to water and to rest, with enemies looking on, and at last to his house (Exodus 15:13; Psalm 78:52–54). The verb is the same one used for the land where "you will lack nothing" (Deuteronomy 8:9).

a: to waters of rest
p: Menuchot means 'rest' or 'resting places', the word for the rest God promised in the land.
b: "Still waters" (KJV) is a good guess, but the Hebrew says "waters of rests", mei menuchot: waters where the flock can rest, or waters that bring rest. Menuchah is the word for the "resting place" the ark sought in the wilderness (Numbers 10:33) and for the rest of the promised land (Deuteronomy 12:9; 1 Kings 8:56). The verb nahal, "guide", is used for leading a flock gently, especially to water (Isaiah 40:11; Isaiah 49:10).

a: He brings my life back
p: The phrase can mean 'revive me' or 'bring me back when I stray'.
b: Nafshi yeshovev is "he brings my nefesh back". As in 19:7 it can mean to revive a fainting life, as water and grass do for sheep. But shuv, "turn back", is also the Bible's word for repentance and for bringing back a lost sheep (Ezekiel 34:16; Jeremiah 50:6). The shepherd both refreshes and fetches home.

a: on the right tracks
p: Ma'gelei tsedeq means tracks that are correct, and also tracks of righteousness.
b: Ma'gal is a well-worn track, like the rut of a cart wheel. Tsedeq can mean "right" in the sense of correct (a right path leads where it should) and "righteousness" in the moral sense. The shepherd leads the sheep on paths that do not end at a cliff, and the psalm lets the moral meaning ring too. He does it "for the sake of his name": his reputation as shepherd is at stake in what happens to his flock.

a: a valley of deep shadow
p: Tsalmavet means 'deep darkness'. The old 'shadow of death' comes from dividing the word in two.
b: Tsalmavet was read by the Greek translators and the KJV as two words, tsel "shadow" and mavet "death", hence "the valley of the shadow of death". Most scholars now take it as one word, "deep darkness" (Job 10:21–22; Amos 5:8), from a root meaning "to be dark"; the site renders it "deep shadow" throughout. Either way it is the darkest place a person can go, and readers have always heard death in it. This is why the psalm is read at funerals in both synagogue and church.

a: Your club and your staff
p: A shepherd carried two tools: a heavy club against wild animals and a long staff to guide and lean on.
b: Shevet is a short, heavy stick or club, used to beat off wolves and lions (1 Samuel 17:34–35) and to count the sheep as they passed under it (Leviticus 27:32; Ezekiel 20:37). Mish'enet is a staff to lean on and to steer the flock. Here they "reassure" the sheep because they mean the shepherd is near. The same word shevet is a king's scepter (2:9; Psalm 45:6) and a rod of discipline (Proverbs 13:24).

a: You lay out a table for me
p: The picture changes from a flock to a guest at a feast. Christians later read it of baptism and the Lord's Supper.
b: In 23:5 the shepherd becomes a host. In the ancient Near East a host who took in a guest was bound to protect him; the guest eats while his enemies can only watch. Oil on the head is the welcome for an honored guest (Luke 7:46), not a king's anointing. Some read the setting as the temple, where a rescued person ate a thanksgiving meal (22:25–26). From the fourth century the newly baptized in Milan and Jerusalem sang this psalm as they went from the font to the anointing and the table: Ambrose (On the Mysteries 8.43) and Cyril of Jerusalem read the table as the Eucharist, the oil as chrism and the cup as the cup of the Lord.

a: will chase after me
p: Radaf is the verb for enemies in pursuit. Here goodness and loyal love do the chasing.
b: Radaf, "pursue", is what enemies do in the Psalms (7:1; 7:5; 31:15). Here the enemies of 23:5 sit and watch, and the ones running after the psalmist are "good things and loyal love" (tov vachesed). The pair often goes together (Psalm 100:5). Hesed, "loyal love", is God's faithfulness to his covenant people.

a: for many long days
p: The Hebrew says 'for length of days', a long life, not 'forever'.
b: Le'orekh yamim, "for length of days", is the phrase for a long life (Deuteronomy 30:20; Psalm 93:5). The KJV's "for ever" is an interpretation, and many Christians and Jews have read the verse as a hope beyond death. The Hebrew itself promises a lifetime near God's house. The same phrase is used in 21:4, where it is paired with "forever and ever".

a: Of David. A psalm.
p: The Greek title adds 'for the first day of the week'. The Mishnah says the Levites sang it in the temple on Sundays.
b: The Mishnah (Tamid 7:4) lists the psalm the Levites sang in the temple each day of the week: Psalm 24 on the first day, 48 on the second, 82 on the third, 94 on the fourth, 81 on the fifth, 93 on the sixth, and 92 on the Sabbath. The Greek title of Psalm 24 (Greek 23) agrees: "for the first day of the week". The Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 31a) explains: on the first day God took possession of the world he made, "the earth is the LORD's". Jews still say Psalm 24 as Sunday's psalm of the day.

a: To the LORD belong the earth and all that fills it
p: Paul quotes this line about food sold in the market. The Talmud uses it to teach blessings before meals.
b: Paul quotes the verse in 1 Corinthians 10:26: a Christian may eat any meat sold in the market, because everything belongs to the Lord. The Talmud (Berakhot 35a) sets this verse beside Psalm 115:16, "the earth is his gift to human beings", and solves the clash: before a blessing everything is the LORD's; after it, it is given to people. So one who enjoys food without saying a blessing is, in effect, stealing from God. The idea that God owns the land lies behind the laws of the jubilee (Leviticus 25:23).

a: upon the seas
p: The ancient picture: land resting on the waters beneath. Canaanite myth told of the storm god defeating the sea.
b: Israel's neighbors pictured the dry land floating on, or held up above, an underground sea. Genesis 1:9–10 and Psalm 136:6 share the picture: God spread out the earth on the waters. In the Canaanite poems from Ugarit the god Baal must fight Yam, "Sea", before he can be king. Psalm 24 does not mention a battle: the LORD simply founded the world on the seas, and they hold it up at his command. The language is shared; the story of a struggle is left out.

a: Who can climb the LORD's mountain?
p: Worshipers ask who may enter, and priests answer. Psalm 15 has the same question and answer.
b: Psalm 24:3–6, like Psalm 15 and Isaiah 33:14–16, seems to be an 'entrance liturgy'. Pilgrims arriving at the temple mount asked who could go up, and a priest at the gate answered with the conditions of the covenant. The answer is not about family, rank or ritual purity, but about hands, heart, worship and speech: clean deeds, honest worship, true oaths. "The LORD's mountain" is Zion, the hill of the temple (Isaiah 2:3).

a: who has not lifted up his soul to what is empty
t: Lifting up the soul to emptiness
p: The phrase echoes the third commandment, against taking up God's name for something empty.
b: Nasa' lashav', "lift up to emptiness", is the language of the third commandment: "You must not take up the name of the LORD your God for something empty" (Exodus 20:7). Shav' means falsehood, emptiness, and often an idol (Jeremiah 18:15). To "lift up the soul" to something is to long for it or rely on it (25:1; Deuteronomy 24:15). So the one who may enter has not given his heart to idols or false oaths. The Leningrad Codex here reads "my soul" (see the variant), which makes the echo of the commandment even closer.

a: Gates, lift your heads high!
p: A procession, probably with the ark, comes to the temple gates. Jews and Christians have read it in many ways.
b: Most scholars think 24:7–10 was sung as the ark, the throne of the LORD, was carried in procession up to the temple, perhaps recalling David's bringing it to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:12–15; Psalm 132:8). The gates are told to raise their "heads", their lintels, as if too low for so great a King. The Talmud (Shabbat 30a) tells how the temple gates would not open for Solomon's ark until he prayed in the name of his father David. Christian tradition sang these verses for Christ's ascension into heaven and for his descent among the dead, breaking open the gates of death; Western and Eastern churches used them at the dedication of a new church, and in some Orthodox churches on Easter night the priest knocks at the closed church doors with these words.
r: 2 Samuel 6:12–15; Psalm 132:8; 1 Kings 8:1–11; Isaiah 26:2; Acts 1:9–11; 1 Peter 3:19

a: the LORD, a warrior in battle
p: The King of glory is the divine warrior of the song at the sea.
b: Gibbor milchamah, "a warrior of battle", recalls the song of Moses: "The LORD is a man of war." (Exodus 15:3). The King coming in has won his battles, perhaps over the waters of 24:2, perhaps over Israel's enemies. This is the same picture as Psalm 18, where the LORD fights for his king, and Isaiah 42:13.

a: The LORD of Armies
p: YHWH tseva'ot, the 'LORD of hosts', is the title of God enthroned on the cherubim above the ark.
b: This is the first time the Psalter uses YHWH tseva'ot. The site renders it "the LORD of Armies" (the KJV's "LORD of hosts"). The "armies" may be Israel's armies (1 Samuel 17:45), the angels (Psalm 103:20–21), or the stars (Isaiah 40:26); the title probably took in all of them. It is closely tied to the ark, the throne of "the LORD of Armies who sits on the cherubim" (1 Samuel 4:4; 2 Samuel 6:2), which supports reading 24:7–10 as an ark procession. The answer is the climax: the King of glory is this LORD.
r: 1 Samuel 4:4; 2 Samuel 6:2; 1 Samuel 17:45; Psalm 103:20–21; Isaiah 6:3; Isaiah 40:26

a: To you, LORD, I raise my soul.
p: Each verse starts with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, with a few gaps and one extra line at the end.
b: Psalm 25 is an acrostic: verse by verse, the first letters run through the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to tav. The pattern is not perfect. The bet line (25:2) puts its letter in the second word, after "My God". There is no clear vav line; 25:5b may once have begun with it. There is no qof: 25:18 and 25:19 both start with resh. And after tav (25:21) comes an extra pe line (25:22), exactly as in Psalm 34, which is built the same way. An acrostic shows completeness, "from A to Z", and was easy to memorize. English cannot show it, and the Plain does not try.
orig: אֵלֶיךָ יְהוָה נַפְשִׁי אֶשָּׂא ('eleikha YHWH nafshi 'essa')

a: I raise my soul
p: To lift the soul to someone is to long for them and depend on them. Psalm 24 used the same phrase.
b: Nafshi 'essa' is "I lift up my nefesh", my life and longing. A poor worker "lifts his soul" to his wages, counting on them (Deuteronomy 24:15). Psalm 24:4 praised the one who has not lifted up his soul to emptiness; Psalm 25 opens by lifting it to the LORD. Psalms 86:4 and 143:8 say the same. The Latin Ad te levavi animam meam is the entrance chant for the first Sunday of Advent in the Roman rite, the first day of the church year.

a: Make me walk in your faithfulness
p: 'Emet means truth, but also faithfulness: what can be relied on.
b: 'Emet comes from the root of "amen", to be firm. It means "truth" and "faithfulness" at once: God's word is true because God is reliable. It pairs with hesed, "loyal love", throughout this psalm (25:10) and in God's own name in Exodus 34:6. To walk in God's 'emet is to live by what he has shown to be reliable. 25:5 is also where the missing vav line of the acrostic may once have begun.

a: The sins I did when young
p: The psalmist asks God not to remember the sins of youth, but to remember him for the sake of his loyal love.
b: Job too complains that God hands him "the guilt of my young days" (Job 13:26). The psalm plays on "remember": do not remember my sins, but remember me. It grounds the request not in the psalmist's goodness but in God's ("because you are good") and in his loyal love. In Sephardic Jewish prayer Psalm 25 is said daily in the supplication prayers (tachanun) after the Amidah.

a: Because of your name, LORD
t: For the sake of the name
p: Forgiveness is asked for the sake of God's own name, as Moses prayed at Sinai.
b: When Israel made the golden calf, Moses asked God to forgive "our guilt and our sin" and God proclaimed his name: merciful, gracious, abounding in loyal love, forgiving guilt (Exodus 34:6–9). The psalmist prays the same way. He admits the guilt is huge and appeals to God's name, God's own character and reputation. The same reasoning comes in 23:3 and 79:9, and in Jeremiah 14:7.

a: The LORD shares his secrets
p: Sod is the circle of close friends and the plans talked over there.
b: Sod means a council or a close circle, and the private talk shared in it. God's prophets stand in his sod (Jeremiah 23:18; Amos 3:7), and "with the upright he shares his secrets" (Proverbs 3:32). Here it belongs to all who fear the LORD: he talks with them as with friends, and shows them his covenant. Jesus says something similar in John 15:15: he calls his disciples friends, because he has told them all he heard from the Father.

a: The troubles of my heart keep spreading
p: The Hebrew says the troubles have 'grown wide'. Many scholars read 'relieve the troubles of my heart'.
b: In Hebrew "wide" is usually good: God gives a person room (4:1; 18:19), while trouble is a "narrow place" (tsarah). The Hebrew here says "the troubles of my heart they have made wide", a strange picture of distress spreading. By joining a letter to the next word, many scholars read harchev, "relieve (widen) the troubles of my heart", which fits the second line; many translations follow that. The Plain keeps the Hebrew, which makes sense as pain that keeps spreading.

a: carry away all my sins
p: The verb nasa' means 'lift' or 'carry'. Forgiving is carrying the load away.
b: Nasa' is the same verb as "raise" in 25:1. To forgive is to lift sin off and carry it away, as the goat on the Day of Atonement "carries" Israel's sins into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:22) and as the servant "carried" the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12). This verse should begin with qof in the acrostic, but begins with resh (re'eh, "look"), like 25:19. Some scholars think it once began with qerav, "draw near".

a: God, ransom Israel
t: An added line for the whole people
p: The last verse stands outside the alphabet, says 'God' and prays for all Israel; many think it was added for worship.
b: The acrostic ended with tav in 25:21. Verse 22 begins with pe, uses Elohim instead of the LORD used everywhere else in the psalm, and turns from one person to all Israel. Psalm 34 ends the same way (34:22). Many critical scholars think the line was added when a personal prayer became a prayer of the congregation, perhaps in exile. Some scholars note that with it the alphabet spells out a pattern found in both psalms: 'aleph, lamed (the middle letter), pe, the letters of the verb 'to learn' ('alaf). Either way, the line shows how one person's prayer was taken up by the whole people.

a: Give judgment for me, LORD
p: The speaker asks God to judge his case, as an accused man would before a court.
b: Shoftini, "judge me", is the plea of someone who wants a verdict: "declare me in the right". Some scholars think Psalm 26 was spoken by a person accused of a crime who came to the temple for God's judgment (compare 1 Kings 8:31–32), or by a priest or Levite at the temple gate (26:6–8). Others read it as the prayer of any worshiper who wants to come before God with a clear conscience. The claim to "integrity" (tom) is a claim of a whole, undivided loyalty to God, not of sinlessness (see 18:20).

a: refine my kidneys and my heart
p: In Hebrew the kidneys stand for the deepest feelings and the heart for the mind and will.
b: The three verbs are words for testing metal: bachan "assay", nissah "try out", tsaraf "refine, smelt". The kelayot, "kidneys", were thought of as the seat of the deepest feelings and secret motives; the lev, "heart", was where a person thinks and decides. God is the one who "tests heart and kidneys" (Jeremiah 11:20; Jeremiah 17:10; Psalm 7:9), and Revelation 2:23 uses the phrase of the risen Christ.

a: two-faced people
p: Na'alamim are 'those who hide themselves', people who conceal what they really are.
b: Na'alamim means "people who are hidden" or "who hide themselves", that is, hypocrites whose real aims are kept out of sight. With "worthless liars" (metei shav', "men of emptiness"; compare 24:4) they make the bad company of 26:4–5, the opposite of the gathering of worshipers in 26:12. Psalm 1:1 makes the same point about whom one sits with.

a: In innocence I wash my hands
p: Washing the hands was a sign of innocence. Pilate did it, and Roman Catholic priests say this verse at Mass.
b: In Deuteronomy 21:6–7 the elders of a town near an unsolved murder wash their hands and declare, "Our hands did not shed this blood." Priests washed before serving at the altar (Exodus 30:19–21). The worshiper here does both: he shows he is innocent and gets ready to go around the altar in procession. Pilate's handwashing at Jesus' trial uses the same sign (Matthew 27:24). In the Roman Mass the priest washes his hands before the Eucharistic prayer; the rite is called the Lavabo, "I will wash", from the Latin of this verse; the priest said 26:6–12 (Vulgate Psalm 25) there until 1970, when Psalm 51:2 replaced it.

a: the place your glory makes its home
p: God's glory 'lived' in the tabernacle and temple. The verb gave later Judaism the word Shekhinah.
b: Mishkan kevodekha, "the dwelling of your glory", uses the word for the tabernacle, mishkan. The glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35) and Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:10–11). From the same root, shakhan, "to dwell", later Jewish teachers called God's presence the Shekhinah. John 1:14 says the Word "pitched his tent" among us and "we saw his glory".

a: The LORD is my light
p: Nowhere else in the Old Testament is God called 'my light' in so many words. Oxford took the Latin as its motto.
b: Light stands for life, safety, joy and truth. Micah 7:8 says, "I sit in the dark, but the LORD is my light," and Isaiah 60:19–20 promises the LORD as Zion's everlasting light. Jesus says "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12), and 1 John 1:5 says "God is light". The Latin of this line, Dominus illuminatio mea, has been the motto of the University of Oxford since the sixteenth century.

a: The LORD is my light and my rescue
t: The psalm of the High Holy Days
p: Jews say Psalm 27 every day from the start of the month of Elul through the autumn festivals.
b: In most Jewish communities Psalm 27 is said twice daily from the first of Elul, a month before Rosh Hashanah, until the end of Sukkot. A midrash (Leviticus Rabbah 21:4) reads "my light" as Rosh Hashanah, the New Year, when God judges the world, and "my rescue" as Yom Kippur, when he forgives. Later writers on Jewish practice added that "he will tuck me into his shelter" (27:5, besukkoh, "in his booth") points to Sukkot, the Feast of Booths. The psalm's mix of confidence and pleading suits the season of repentance.

a: to eat my flesh
p: The picture is of wild beasts, but 'eating someone's pieces' was also a phrase for slander.
b: Le'ekhol 'et-besari, "to eat my flesh", pictures attackers as beasts of prey (compare 22:13; Micah 3:3). In Aramaic, "to eat someone's pieces" means to accuse or slander them (Daniel 3:8; Daniel 6:24), and the false witnesses of 27:12 suggest that slander is part of the attack. The Bible's "flesh" (basar) is the living body, not just meat.

a: to look at how lovely the LORD is
p: No'am is pleasantness or delight. Levaqqer means to look closely, inquire, or seek guidance.
b: No'am is pleasantness, kindness and beauty together (Psalm 90:17; Proverbs 3:17). To "look at" (chazah, used of prophetic vision) the LORD's loveliness in the temple may mean to see his presence in the worship there. Levaqqer is less certain: "to inquire" (to ask God for guidance, perhaps through a priest), "to look carefully" (as a priest examines a sacrifice, Leviticus 13:36), or "to be there in the morning" (boqer). Christian writers from Augustine on read the verse as the soul's longing for the vision of God (Matthew 5:8; 1 Corinthians 13:12).

a: My heart repeats your word to me
p: The Hebrew reads literally 'To you my heart said, "Seek (plural) my face."' Translators patch it in different ways.
b: The Hebrew is very short and odd: "To you said my heart, 'Seek my face', your face, LORD, I will seek." The command "seek" is plural, and "my face" seems to be God's. Translators patch it in three main ways: "My heart says of you, 'Seek his face'"; "You said, 'Seek my face'; my heart says to you, 'Your face I will seek'"; or, as the Plain does, the heart repeats God's own command back to him. The Greek goes its own way: "my heart said to you, my face has sought you" (Rahlfs 26:8). Whatever the grammar, the sense is clear: God invited his people to seek his face (2 Chronicles 7:14), and the psalmist takes him at his word.
orig: לְךָ אָמַר לִבִּי בַּקְּשׁוּ פָנָי (lekha 'amar libbi baqqeshu fanai)

a: the LORD will gather me in
p: The verb is used for taking a homeless person into one's house, or gathering the dead to their family.
b: 'Asaf, "gather in", is what the old man of Gibeah should have done for travelers in the square (Judges 19:15). If even parents, the people most bound to care for a child, give up on him, God will take him into his house. Isaiah 49:15 asks whether a mother can forget her nursing child: even if she could, God will not. Some think the line means real rejection by family; others that it is a way of saying "even in the worst case".

a: a witness who breathes out violence
p: Yafeach may be a word for 'witness', known from Ugarit and from Proverbs.
b: The Hebrew vifeach chamas is usually translated "and they breathe out violence". But Proverbs uses a word yafiach as a parallel to "witness" (Proverbs 6:19; Proverbs 14:5; Proverbs 14:25), and a word yph, "witness", appears in the texts from Ugarit. So the line probably means "a witness of violence", one who "breathes out" lies that lead to violence. The law of Moses demanded two or three honest witnesses and punished false ones (Deuteronomy 19:15–19).

a: toward the inner room of your holy place
p: The devir was the innermost room of the temple, where the ark stood. Israelites raised their hands toward it to pray.
b: Devir is the name of the inner room of Solomon's temple, the Most Holy Place, where the ark and the cherubim were (1 Kings 6:5; 1 Kings 6:16–23; 1 Kings 8:6). Solomon's prayer asks God to hear those who pray "toward this place" (1 Kings 8:29–30), and Daniel later prayed toward Jerusalem from Babylon (Daniel 6:10). Raising open hands was the normal posture of prayer (Exodus 9:29; 1 Timothy 2:8).

a: who say "Peace" to their neighbors
p: The wicked greet their neighbors with 'Shalom' while planning harm.
b: Shalom was, and still is, the everyday Hebrew greeting. Jeremiah 9:8 says the same of his people: each one speaks peace to his neighbor but sets an ambush in his heart. Joab greeted Amasa with "Is it well (shalom) with you, my brother?" and stabbed him (2 Samuel 20:9–10). Judas greeted Jesus with a kiss (Matthew 26:49).

a: Give them what matches their work
p: The psalmist asks God to pay the wicked back. Jews and Christians have read such prayers in different ways.
b: The request is for justice in kind: let their deeds come back on them. It is not a request for personal revenge; it leaves judgment to God (Deuteronomy 32:35), and the next verse says God will do it. The New Testament uses the same language for God's judgment (Romans 2:6; 2 Timothy 4:14; Revelation 18:6), while also telling believers not to take revenge themselves (Romans 12:19). Some Christians pray such lines against evil powers rather than people; some liturgies leave them out. The site's page on the curse psalms gives the range of practice.

a: Shepherd them, and carry them
p: The psalm ends by asking God to shepherd and carry his people. The church took the line into the Te Deum.
b: Isaiah 40:11 pictures God as a shepherd who gathers the lambs and carries them in his arms, and Isaiah 63:9 says God lifted and carried his people all the days of old. The last line of this psalm, in Latin Salvum fac populum tuum, Domine, et benedic hereditati tuae, became one of the closing lines of the hymn Te Deum, sung in Western churches since the fourth or fifth century: "O Lord, save thy people, and bless thine heritage" in the old English version.

a: you sons of the gods
p: Bene 'elim means the heavenly beings around God's throne. They are called to worship him.
b: Bene 'elim, "sons of gods", are the members of God's heavenly court, elsewhere called "the sons of God" (Job 1:6) or "the holy ones" (Psalm 89:5–7). The Canaanite texts from Ugarit speak of the bn ilm, the sons of El, the gods of the pantheon. In Psalm 29 they are not rivals but worshipers, told to give the LORD the glory. Jewish and Christian readers have understood them as angels. The Greek has a double line here (see the variant).
r: Job 1:6; Psalm 89:5–7; Psalm 82:1; Psalm 103:20; Deuteronomy 32:8; Revelation 4:8–11

a: in holy splendor
p: Hadrat qodesh may be holy clothing, the splendor of the holy place, or 'when the Holy One appears'.
b: Hadrat qodesh appears also in Psalm 96:9 and 1 Chronicles 16:29. Three readings are common: worship "in holy attire" (as priests wore holy garments, Exodus 28:2), "in the splendor of holiness" (God's or the sanctuary's), or, from a Ugaritic word hdrt meaning a vision or appearance, "when the Holy One appears", which fits the storm that follows. The Greek has "in his holy court" (Rahlfs 28:2), reading chatsrat, "court", for hadrat. The KJV's "beauty of holiness" has become a well-known phrase in English.

a: The LORD's voice is over the waters.
p: Psalm 29 uses the language of the Canaanite storm god Baal. Scholars debate whether it was adapted from a Baal hymn.
b: Seven times the psalm says qol YHWH, "the LORD's voice", which in Hebrew is also the word for thunder. In the Ugaritic poems Baal "gives his holy voice" and the earth shakes; his mountains are Lebanon and Sirion (Hermon), his rival is Sea, and he is enthroned as king. In 1935 H. L. Ginsberg argued that Psalm 29 is "a Phoenician hymn" with the LORD's name put in for Baal's, and F. M. Cross and others agreed. Others, such as Craigie, think Israel wrote it in its neighbors' style to say that the storm belongs to the LORD, not Baal. The likeness is real; whether it is a reworked hymn or a deliberate answer cannot be proved. Either way, the psalm denies Baal everything his worshipers gave him.
orig: קוֹל יְהוָה (qol YHWH), 'the voice / thunder of the LORD'

a: Sirion
p: The storm comes in off the sea, crashes into Lebanon and Hermon, and dies away in the desert.
b: The psalm follows a real storm's track. It begins over "the vast waters" of the Mediterranean (29:3), strikes the cedars of Lebanon (29:5), shakes Lebanon and Sirion, the Sidonian name for Mount Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:9), and passes into "the wilderness of Kadesh" (29:8). Kadesh may be Kadesh-barnea in the far south, so that the storm sweeps the whole land from north to south, or Kadesh on the Orontes River in Syria, near Lebanon; a Ugaritic text also mentions a "wilderness of Kadesh". Lebanon and Sirion were Phoenician mountains, the heart of Baal's country.

a: makes the does go into labor
p: The Hebrew says the LORD's voice makes the does give birth. Changing the vowels gives 'twists the oaks'.
b: Yecholel 'ayyalot as pointed means "makes the does writhe (in labor)". With other vowels, 'elot, "great trees, oaks", the line reads "twists the oaks", which pairs with "strips the forests bare" and is followed by many translations. Ancient people believed that terror could bring on birth (compare 1 Samuel 4:19), and Job 39:1–3 names the calving of the deer as one of God's secrets. The Plain keeps the Hebrew vowels.

a: everyone says, "Glory!"
p: Jews sing Psalm 29 to welcome the Sabbath and when the Torah scroll is returned on Sabbath mornings.
b: In his temple, heavenly or earthly, all cry "Glory!" The psalm has a large place in Jewish prayer. It is one of the psalms of Kabbalat Shabbat, the Friday evening service that welcomes the Sabbath, and it is sung on Sabbath mornings as the Torah scroll is carried back to the ark. The Talmud (Berakhot 28b) says the eighteen blessings of the daily Amidah match the eighteen times the LORD's name is said in this psalm.

a: At the Flood the LORD took his throne
p: Mabbul is the word for Noah's Flood and is used nowhere else outside Genesis 6–11.
b: Mabbul is the special word for the Flood of Genesis 6–11; it does not appear anywhere else in the Old Testament. So the psalm points back to Noah's day: the LORD sat as King over the waters then, and he sits as King forever. In the Canaanite myths Baal won his throne by defeating Sea; in this psalm the LORD needs no battle. He simply sits enthroned over the flood.

a: the LORD will bless his people with peace
t: The last word of the Mishnah
p: The storm ends in shalom. The Mishnah closes with this very verse.
b: After the thunder, the last word is shalom, peace and wholeness, the blessing of the priests (Numbers 6:26). The Mishnah, the great collection of Jewish law made about AD 200, ends with it: God found no vessel that could hold blessing for Israel except peace, as it says, "the LORD will bless his people with peace" (Mishnah Uktsin 3:12). The verse is also said at the end of the grace after meals.

a: A song for the dedication of the house.
p: A personal psalm of healing is titled for the dedication of 'the house'. Readers have suggested several houses.
b: The psalm itself is a thanksgiving for healing from a near-fatal illness. The title ties it to the chanukkat habbayit, "the dedication of the house". Suggestions include David's palace (2 Samuel 5:11), the site of the future temple, which David bought after the plague (1 Chronicles 21:18–22:1), Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:63), the second temple (Ezra 6:16) and its rededication by Judas Maccabeus in 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:52–59), which is the feast of Hanukkah. The rabbinic tract Soferim (chapter 18) names Psalm 30 as the psalm for Hanukkah, and since the 1600s many Jewish prayer books also have it every morning, just before the morning psalms. Many scholars think the title was added when one person's thanks became the song of the rebuilt temple.
r: 2 Samuel 5:11; 1 Chronicles 21:18–22:1; 1 Kings 8:63; Ezra 6:16; 1 Maccabees 4:52–59; John 10:22

a: for you drew me up
p: Dillah is the verb for drawing water up from a well with a bucket.
b: Dillitani, "you drew me up", uses the verb for drawing water from a well (Exodus 2:16; Exodus 2:19; Proverbs 20:5). The psalmist pictures himself at the bottom of a deep pit (30:3; 30:9), and God pulls him up like a bucket. Jeremiah was pulled up out of a cistern with ropes (Jeremiah 38:13).

a: his favor is for life
p: The Hebrew sets 'a moment' against 'life'. It can mean his favor lasts a lifetime, or that his favor gives life.
b: Rega' be'appo, chayyim birtsono: "a moment in his anger, life in his favor". Most take "life" as "a lifetime", the opposite of "a moment" (compare Isaiah 54:7–8, "for a little moment I abandoned you"). Others read it as "in his favor is life", as the Greek does. Both say that God's anger is the exception and his goodwill the rule. The next lines turn the same thought into a picture: weeping is a guest who stays the night and leaves in the morning.

a: in my comfortable days I said
t: The sin of being too sure
p: The psalmist confesses that in good times he thought nothing could shake him.
b: Beshalvi, "in my ease", is security that forgets God (compare Deuteronomy 8:11–18; Proverbs 30:8–9). The wicked say the same thing, "I will not totter" (Psalm 10:6). The illness taught the psalmist that his firm mountain stood only by God's favor (30:7). Many readers connect this with David's census, done in pride, which brought the plague that ended at the threshing floor where the temple was later built (2 Samuel 24; 1 Chronicles 21), and so with the title.

a: you set strength on my mountain
p: The Hebrew is hard. 'My mountain' may be Zion, the psalmist's high position, or simply his firm footing.
b: The Hebrew reads "you made stand for my mountain strength". "My mountain" may be Mount Zion, if the speaker is a king; or a figure for a strong, high position (compare 18:33, "my high places"); or, by a small change, the Greek's "to my beauty (hadari) you gave strength". All agree on the sense: God's favor, not the psalmist's own strength, kept him standing, and when God hid his face he fell into panic.

a: Can dust give you thanks?
p: The psalmist argues that God loses a worshiper if he dies. The Psalms often say the dead cannot praise God.
b: The prayer is bold: what would God gain from a dead servant? Dust cannot praise him. Several psalms say the same (6:5; Psalm 88:10–12; Psalm 115:17), as does Hezekiah's prayer when he recovered from illness (Isaiah 38:18–19). For most of the Old Testament, Sheol is a place of silence, cut off from the worship of the temple. Later Jewish and Christian teaching on resurrection and on the dead with God (Daniel 12:2; Philippians 1:23) changed how these lines were read. For how churches differ on the state of the dead, see 6:5.

a: you untied my sackcloth
p: Mourners wore sackcloth, rough goat-hair cloth tied at the waist. God untied it and 'belted' him with joy instead.
b: Saq was coarse cloth of goat hair, worn by mourners and by people praying in distress (2 Samuel 3:31; 1 Kings 21:27; Esther 4:1). The sick psalmist had put it on. Now God "loosed" it and "girded" him, wrapped him around the waist, with joy. Mispad, "mourning", is the wailing at a funeral; machol, "dancing", the round dance at a festival (Exodus 15:20; Judges 21:21; Jeremiah 31:13).

a: so that glory may make music to you
p: Kavod, 'glory', here probably means the self, perhaps with a play on kaved, 'liver'.
b: In several psalms "my glory" stands for the self or the soul (Psalm 16:9; Psalm 57:8; Psalm 108:1; Genesis 49:6). Many scholars think it is a play on kaved, "liver", which, like the kidneys and heart, was thought of as a seat of feeling (Lamentations 2:11). The Hebrew here has only "glory", without "my"; the Greek has "my glory", and many scholars read kevodi "my glory" or kevedi "my liver" (see the variant). The Plain keeps the Hebrew. The point is that the whole person, once nearly silenced in death, will now sing without stopping.
